final_answer:
Merge sort works by recursively dividing the list into halves until each sublist contains one element (base case). Then, it merges adjacent sorted sublists by comparing their front elements and appending the smaller one to a new list. This process continues until the entire list is merged into one sorted list. Merge sort has a guaranteed O(n log n) time complexity and is stable.

For linked lists, merge sort is preferred over quicksort because:  
1) quicksort relies on random access (common in arrays) and has O(n) partitioning overhead in linked lists, while merge sort uses sequential traversal and pointer adjustments.  
2) quicksort’s worst-case O(n²) is riskier for linked lists, whereas merge sort maintains O(n log n) regardless.  
3) merging linked lists can be done in-place with pointer changes, minimizing memory overhead compared to quicksort’s recursive stacks and potential worst-case memory fragmentation.
